To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the deployment of man-made reefs in the Mediterranean Sea resulted in a 68 fold biomass increase of benthic sedentaries, with no significant changes in the biomass of mobile species and pelagic zooplankton feeders, and that the increase in fish biomass was supported by a local OM production and the attraction of pelagic species.

(1) the biomass of fish on artificial reefs (ARs), deployed in temperate waters, was dominated by benthic sedentaries and increased over time, (2) changes in fish community composition and biomass were driven by the combined effect of production and attraction, and (3) the isotopic signature of fish on ARs revealed the importance of local organic matter sources and the attraction of pelagic species to ARs.

the deployment of man-made rocky substrates can be an effective management tool to increase fish biomass production, but this effect can be highly variable depending on the specific functional components of the fish community.
the deployment of artificial reefs can be used to enhance fish production, but this effect is highly dependent on the functional traits of the target species and on the environmental conditions.
